segments.text: Welcome to Earth's Atmosphere and Weather Systems. In this lesson, we examine the layers of gas protecting our planet.
The atmosphere consists primarily of seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen, with trace gases like argon and carbon dioxide.
The lowest layer is the troposphere, extending up to twelve kilometers, where nearly all terrestrial weather occurs.
Above the troposphere lies the stratosphere, home to the ozone layer which absorbs harmful solar ultraviolet radiation.
The mesosphere is the third layer, where incoming meteors burn up due to friction with atmospheric particles.
Higher still is the thermosphere, characterized by rapidly rising temperatures and the display of brilliant auroras.
Finally, the exosphere forms the outermost boundary, gradually merging into the vacuum of interplanetary space.
Solar energy warms the equatorial regions more intensely than polar regions, creating planetary temperature gradients.
These temperature differences drive atmospheric circulation cells, generating prevailing winds across the globe.
The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects moving air masses to the right in the northern hemisphere.
High pressure systems generally bring clear skies and cool air, while low pressure systems foster clouds and precipitation.
Jet streams are fast, narrow air currents flowing eastward near the tropopause that steer major storm tracks.
Humidity represents the amount of water vapor in the air, condensing into clouds when saturated air cools.
Understanding these dynamical systems enables meteorologists to forecast extreme weather and protect communities.
